assignments.title: 1.8 Critical Questions: Lodge, Speech Against the League of Nations
assignments.html:
Read the Lodge speech, then answer all four questions. Write three to five sentences for each. Use evidence from the speech and from Lesson 1.1. A strong answer gives a reason, not just an opinion. If your answer depends on something you cannot know, say so.

1. Suppose Wilson had accepted Lodge's change to Article 10 in the fall of 1919, and the Senate had approved the League with that change. Would the League have been stronger or weaker with the United States as a member under those conditions? Explain your reasoning.

2. Lodge was not one of the senators who opposed the League on any terms, yet his objection to Article 10 persuaded many senators who were. Why did an argument about one article carry so much weight in the Senate?

3. Lodge's argument rests on an idea about who should hold the power to commit a nation to war. What is that idea, and why would a citizen of a republic care about it?

4. Suppose the Senate had approved the League without any changes. Would the United States have been better or worse off in the 1920s? Defend your answer with at least one specific consequence.

Submit: type your answers in the text box in Canvas and submit.

assignments.title: 1.9 Primary Source Exercise: Palmer, "The Case Against the 'Reds'"
assignments.html:
Read the Palmer article, then answer all four questions. Write three to five sentences for each. Use evidence from the article and from Lesson 1.3. A strong answer gives a reason, not just an opinion.

1. Palmer wrote in 1920 as if revolution had been close. What events of 1919 made his warning believable to many Americans, even those who had never met a radical?

2. Palmer defends the raids as the way to protect the country. Which principle about how a republic should treat people it accuses of crimes is missing from his defense? Use an example from the raids to show why that principle matters.

3. Palmer predicted violence for May 1, 1920, and nothing happened. Suppose instead that bombs had gone off in several cities that day. How would the Red Scare, and Palmer's reputation, probably have been different? Explain.

4. Palmer wrote to persuade readers, not only to inform them. What in the article shows this? Then name one kind of evidence from outside the article that you would want to check before trusting his claims.

Submit: type your answers in the text box in Canvas and submit.

questions.text: Ford's Five-Dollar Day paid about double the usual factory wage. Which statement best explains why it was good for his business as well as for his workers?

It forced his rivals to charge higher prices for their cars.
It made the assembly line unnecessary.

questions.text: Mass production made goods cheap, yet the lesson says a new problem appeared. What was it?

Workers refused to learn the new jobs.
Families stopped wanting cars and radios.
Factories could make more goods than families could pay for in cash.

questions.text: General Motors passed Ford as the top seller in 1927. Which change in the market best explains why?

answers.text: Buyers who already owned a car wanted color, style, and a better model to move up to, and Ford kept selling one plain car.

The government began to favor General Motors.

Credit would make banks too powerful to be regulated.

questions.text: In 1935, Italy invaded Ethiopia. Congress had just passed a Neutrality Act banning weapon sales to countries at war. What was the effect of this law on Ethiopia?

answers.text: The United States sold weapons to Ethiopia but not to Italy.
The United States sent its navy to protect Ethiopia.
The League of Nations took over the sale of American weapons.
Ethiopia could not buy American weapons any more easily than Italy could.

questions.text: Neville Chamberlain came home from Munich and said he had brought "peace for our time." Which later event best shows that his claim was wrong?

answers.text: Czechoslovakia was invited to the next meeting with Hitler.
Hitler broke his promise to ask for nothing more by taking the rest of Czechoslovakia six months later.
The League of Nations punished Germany for the Sudetenland.
Britain and France sent armies into the Rhineland.

questions.text: The "cash and carry" policy let Britain and France buy American weapons if they paid in full and carried the goods away in their own ships. Why did this policy help the Allies much more than Germany?

answers.text: The Allies did not have to pay for the weapons.
Congress ordered American factories to sell only to the Allies.
The British navy controlled the Atlantic, so only the Allies could carry the goods across it.
Germany refused to buy American weapons.

questions.text: By late 1940, Britain was running out of money, yet it still needed weapons. How did Lend-Lease solve this problem?

answers.text: It let Britain receive weapons without paying cash on the spot.
It forced Britain to sell its colonies to the United States.
It ended the draft in the United States.
It sent American soldiers to fight in Britain at once.

questions.text: In 1938, Roosevelt worked hard to stop a proposed amendment that would require a national vote before any declaration of war. Which concern did many supporters of the amendment hold?

answers.text: That the Navy was too large for peacetime.
That Britain would refuse to fight without American help.
That a president might take the country into war without the people's say.
That the Constitution should be rewritten to remove Congress's war power.

questions.text: After Roosevelt froze Japanese money and cut off oil, why were Japan's leaders in such a hard position?

answers.text: Japan imported most of its oil from the United States, so they had to give up their conquests in China or seize oil elsewhere by force.
Japan had no army left to fight with.
The League of Nations had ordered Japan to leave Manchuria.
Roosevelt had promised to stop the embargo if Japan attacked Hawaii.

questions.text: Hitler declared war on the United States three days after Pearl Harbor, though no treaty required him to. Which statement best describes the importance of this choice?

answers.text: It ended the war in the Pacific.
It placed the United States in a war with all three Axis powers, instead of letting it focus on Japan alone.
It allowed Britain to leave the war.
It gave Congress no reason to declare war on Japan.

questions.text: In September 1940, Roosevelt traded fifty old destroyers to Britain without a vote of Congress. Why did some people say he had gone too far?

answers.text: A major step toward war, taken without Congress, struck critics as a president taking power the Constitution gives to Congress.
The ships were too new to give away.

quizzes.description: Choose the best answer to each question. Some questions ask you to put together facts from different parts of the course.

questions.text: Senator Lodge wanted changes to Article 10 of the League Covenant. What was his main fear?

answers.text: That the League would make the United States pay Germany's war debts after the peace was signed.
That the promise to defend other members could draw the nation into war without a vote of Congress.
That the League would be allowed to collect taxes from American citizens through its Assembly.
That the Senate would lose its power to approve every future treaty with a foreign nation.

questions.text: Which set of events best explains why the Red Scare faded by 1920?

answers.text: Congress passed a law forbidding the arrest of anarchists, and Palmer was soon elected president of the nation that year.
The Bolsheviks gave up power in Russia, and the strikes in American cities ended on their own that year.
The Supreme Court ruled the Palmer Raids lawful, and so the public quickly lost interest in the whole matter.
An official canceled many deportation orders, judges criticized the raids, and Palmer's predicted May 1 violence never came.

questions.text: The Immigration Act of 1924 used 1890 as its starting date instead of 1910. Why did this favor immigrants from northern and western Europe?

answers.text: Far fewer southern and eastern Europeans were living in the country in 1890, so their quotas were smaller.
Most immigrants from northern and western Europe had arrived after 1890, so their quotas would be larger.
The census of 1890 had not counted anyone who had come from southern or eastern Europe at all.
The law gave larger quotas to countries that had fought on the winning side in the Great War.

questions.text: Henry Ford introduced the Five-Dollar Day in 1914. Why was it good business for Ford?

answers.text: It let Ford close his Sociological Department and stop checking on how his workers lived at home.
It forced his rivals to stop using assembly lines and return to building each car in one spot.
It cut costly turnover from workers who kept quitting, and gave workers pay to buy the cars they built.
It lowered the price of the Model T to below one hundred dollars so that every family could afford to buy one.

questions.text: General Motors passed Ford as the nation's top seller in 1927. Which choice best explains this?

answers.text: Sloan offered a ladder of brands, bright colors, and yearly style changes, while Ford kept one plain car.
General Motors sold its cars at a lower price than the Model T, and it never sold them on credit.
Ford refused to build cars with gasoline engines, and the government ordered his plants closed for good.
General Motors invented the assembly line in 1913, and Ford had not yet learned how to use it.

questions.text: Critics worried about the growth of installment buying in the 1920s. Which concern did they raise?

answers.text: Credit made goods so cheap that factories could no longer earn a profit on the cars they built.
Credit pulls future income into the present, so spending came to depend on pay that might vanish.
Credit was offered only to the wealthy, so that radios and cars stayed out of reach for most families.
Credit was forbidden by the Constitution, and every debt had to be repaid in gold within a year.

questions.text: What did the failure of Prohibition show about law?

answers.text: A law that bans a harmful habit will always cut that habit by half, even if few agents enforce it.
A constitutional amendment cannot be repealed once the states have ratified it and Congress has funded it.
Enforcement works best when it is left to local police and is taken out of the hands of federal agents.
A law needs the support of those it governs, and when many treat it as a joke, respect for all law suffers.

questions.text: The election of 1928 put the split between city and country on the ballot. Which description is correct?

answers.text: Hoover, a Catholic from New York, won the big cities, while Smith, a Protestant, won the farm states.
Smith, a supporter of Prohibition, won the South, while Hoover, a Catholic, carried the North and West by a wide margin.
Smith, a Catholic and opponent of Prohibition, drew city voters, while Hoover, a Prohibition supporter, won big.
Smith and Hoover both opposed Prohibition, and Hoover won because he had grown up on an Iowa farm.

questions.text: W. E. B. Du Bois criticized Marcus Garvey sharply. Which difference between the two men is correct?

answers.text: Du Bois urged Black Americans to move to Africa, while Garvey worked inside the Democratic Party for civil rights.
Du Bois sought full citizenship in the United States, while Garvey urged pride and Black-owned business.
Du Bois led the Harlem Renaissance as a poet, while Garvey led the Ku Klux Klan in the northern states.
Du Bois favored Prohibition as a sincere reform, while Garvey wanted the 18th Amendment to be repealed.

questions.text: The stock market crash has been called "the match," with the fuel piling up for years. Which pair best describes the fuel?

answers.text: Banks made poor loans, and with no deposit insurance, rumors could set off runs that ruined even healthy banks.
Most American families owned stock, and the Federal Reserve had printed far too much money in 1929.
Congress had cut tariffs to zero, and other countries therefore stopped buying American goods in the year 1930.
Farmers had gone out of business in 1920, and factories had stopped making cars and radios altogether.

questions.text: Over the protest of more than a thousand economists, Hoover signed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff in 1930. What happened next?

answers.text: Foreign governments lowered their tariffs in return, and American exports doubled within about two years.
The tariff raised so much money that the budget came into balance, and the closed banks soon reopened.
The tariff forced European nations to pay their war debts early, which ended the gold standard for good.
Other countries raised their own tariffs, trade collapsed, and American farms and factories lost buyers abroad.

questions.text: Why did the clearing of the Bonus Army hurt Hoover so badly?

answers.text: The Senate had just voted to pay the bonus, and Hoover vetoed the bill on the same day the Army moved.
The marchers had refused to leave the Capitol and attacked police with weapons, which quickly turned the press against them.
Newsreels showed soldiers driving veterans out, MacArthur went past Hoover's orders, and most marchers were real veterans.
The Army fired on veterans in every large city, and Hoover personally ordered that the camp be set on fire.

questions.text: The Emergency Banking Act ended the banking panic quickly. Which two steps best explain this?

answers.text: Every bank, sound or not, was reopened at once, and the government promised to pay every depositor in cash.
Congress created deposit insurance and abolished the Federal Reserve in the same afternoon session.
The president closed the stock market for a year and lent each family a month's wages out of the Treasury.
Only sound banks reopened, and Roosevelt explained the plan to the country by radio in simple words.

questions.text: Which complaint would a member of the American Liberty League most likely have made about the New Deal?

answers.text: It threatened property, freedom, and the Constitution, and it put too much power in the hands of Washington.
It did not limit private fortunes or give every family a home and a basic income, as Huey Long wanted.
It should pay every American over the age of sixty two hundred dollars a month, as Dr. Townsend proposed.
It moved too slowly in helping farm workers and factory workers to join unions and to bargain.

questions.text: Justice Brandeis wrote that a state may serve as a "laboratory" for new ideas. Which event best shows his point?

answers.text: The states ratified the 21st Amendment through special conventions of voters in 1933, which ended the ban on alcohol.
Wisconsin passed unemployment insurance in 1932, and the nation later built a system on lessons from such tests.
The Agricultural Adjustment Act paid farmers across the nation to grow less so that crop prices would rise.
The Tennessee Valley Authority built dams on one river to control floods and to make cheap electric power.

questions.text: Roosevelt designed Social Security as insurance paid by payroll taxes instead of as a gift. What was his reason?

answers.text: The Constitution forbade the national government from giving money directly to any citizen of the country.
Southern senators demanded that the program pay no benefits at all until the year 1950 had arrived.
Workers who paid in would feel they had earned benefits, and no later Congress could easily end them.
Business owners wanted to pay the whole cost themselves so they could control how the plan was run.

questions.text: In Schechter Poultry v. United States, the Court struck down the National Industrial Recovery Act. Which pair of reasons did it give?

answers.text: The law raised taxes without a vote of the House, and it banned all labor unions across the country at once.
It gave too much power to the president and industry groups, and a local Brooklyn sale was not interstate trade.
The law had been passed in a single afternoon, and the president had never signed it into law at all.
The law let the states regulate trade with foreign nations, and it had been written by the Brain Trust.

questions.text: Roosevelt's plan to add justices to the Supreme Court failed even after his landslide win in 1936. Which choice best explains why?

answers.text: The Constitution fixes the Court at nine justices, so Congress had no power at all to pass the bill.
The Court struck down the bill as soon as Congress passed it, in a vote of six to three in 1937.
The Four Horsemen resigned together that spring, so Roosevelt no longer felt any need for the plan to go forward.
Many Americans saw it as an attack on the judges' independence, and the Court began upholding New Deal laws without it.

questions.text: The Neutrality Acts of 1935 to 1937 were meant to keep America out of war. Why did they fail to help countries attacked by aggressors?

answers.text: They banned arms sales to all countries at war, so a victim could buy no more easily than the attacker.
They allowed arms sales only to the Axis nations, so the victims had to buy their weapons from their own enemies.
They sent American troops to every war zone in Europe in order to keep the sea lanes open.
They took away the power of Congress to declare war and gave it to the League of Nations.

questions.text: In 1941, Roosevelt cut off oil to Japan. What choice did this force on Japan's leaders?

answers.text: To buy oil from Germany or else to make a separate peace with the Soviet Union that summer.
To ask the League of Nations for help or else to leave the pact with Germany and Italy.
To give up their conquests in China or else to take the oil of Southeast Asia by force.
To move their fleet to Hawaii for good or else to close the Panama Canal to American ships.

questions.text: Britain and France agreed at Munich to let Germany take the Sudetenland. What was the result?

answers.text: Czechoslovakia joined the League of Nations and was defended by the army of France in the spring.
Germany returned the Rhineland to France in exchange, and Hitler agreed to disband his air force.
The United States joined the agreement and promised to send troops to guard the new border.
Hitler's promise was broken within six months, when his troops took the rest of Czechoslovakia.

questions.text: Roosevelt and Churchill agreed to defeat Germany first and hold Japan back. What was their reasoning?

answers.text: Japan had already been beaten at Pearl Harbor and needed no further fighting for the next two years.
Germany was stronger, and if it beat the Soviet Union and Britain, it would control Europe's industry.
Germany had the only army that could land troops on the American coast and march on Washington.
The American people had demanded that Europe come first, and Congress had voted to make it law.

questions.text: Which factors best explain the American victory at Midway?

answers.text: Codebreakers learned the target, Nimitz had carriers ready, and planes struck while Japanese decks were crowded.
The American fleet had far more battleships, and Japan had built no aircraft carriers of its own at that time.
MacArthur's army landed on Midway and forced the Japanese fleet to withdraw before the battle began.
Japan's fleet ran out of fuel on its way to the island, and its pilots refused to attack.

questions.text: Reports of the Nazi plan to murder the Jews reached the United States in 1942. Which statement best describes the response?

answers.text: Congress opened the borders to all refugees in 1942, and the Army bombed the railways that led to the camps.
The government refused to believe the reports until American soldiers reached the camps in the spring of 1945.
The Bermuda conference of 1943 settled the refugee question, and rescue ships sailed from every Atlantic port.
The news was confirmed in 1942, but action stayed limited until a Treasury report led to the War Refugee Board.

questions.text: Which statement best summarizes the history of Executive Order 9066 and Korematsu v. United States?

answers.text: The Court struck the order down in 1944, and no one was ever removed from a home on the West Coast.
Congress ordered the removal in a law passed in 1942, and the Court has upheld that law ever since then.
The Court allowed it in 1944 as a military necessity, and Congress later apologized and paid survivors.
The order applied only to Japanese citizens, and every one of them was convicted of spying for Japan.

questions.text: The Battle of Okinawa mattered to Truman's decision about the atomic bomb. Why?

answers.text: It showed what invading Japan might cost: over twelve thousand Americans died, and kamikaze attacks sank dozens of ships.
It proved that Japan's navy was still strong enough to invade Hawaii and to cut the American supply lines at sea.
It showed that the Soviet Union would not join the war against Japan, whatever the Allies had promised at Yalta.
It ended the war in Europe at last and freed millions of troops to be sent to the Pacific.

questions.text: Which pair of events from August 1945 best shows the role of contingency?

answers.text: The Enola Gay was built in New Mexico, and the Soviet Union declared war on Japan on the same day.
Clouds covered Kokura, so the second bomb fell on Nagasaki, and the emperor broke a tie in Japan's war council.
Truman met Stalin at Potsdam, and the Potsdam Declaration was issued by the United States, Britain, and China.
The firebombing of Tokyo killed 100,000 people, and Japan's navy was lost in the Battle of Leyte Gulf.

questions.text: The United Nations Security Council gave each of five nations a permanent seat and a veto. Why did this design make it likely that the council would sometimes be unable to act?

answers.text: The General Assembly could overrule any decision of the council.
Any one of the five could block a decision, so when the great powers disagreed, nothing could be done.
The council had no power to order action to keep the peace.
Only members of the General Assembly were allowed to vote.

questions.text: The Senate approved the United Nations Charter by 89 to 2, though it had rejected the League of Nations in 1919. Which fact from the lesson best helps explain the difference?

answers.text: The United Nations had no power to act.
The Senate had changed its mind about Woodrow Wilson.

questions.text: The Bretton Woods Conference tied other currencies to the dollar and the dollar to gold. Which problem from the 1930s was this meant to prevent?

answers.text: Tariff wars and money troubles that choked trade.
A shortage of American soldiers.
The spread of communism in Asia.
The end of the Marshall Plan.

questions.text: At Yalta, Stalin promised "free and unfettered elections" in Poland. What does the lesson's account of Eastern Europe after 1945 suggest about that promise?

answers.text: It was kept in every country the Red Army entered.
It was kept in Poland but broken in Czechoslovakia.
It meant very little, since elections were rigged or put off and local communists took control.
It was canceled by a vote of the United Nations.

questions.text: Between 1945 and 1947, the armed forces shrank from about twelve million to fewer than two million. What was one result?

answers.text: The United States had far less force in Europe than the Soviet army, even though its factories were far larger.
The United States left Europe completely, as it had in 1919.
The Soviet Union demobilized at the same speed.
Congress ended the draft permanently.

questions.text: Kennan argued that Soviet leaders were cautious and would back away when they met firm resistance. Which action best fits a policy built on that belief?

answers.text: Pulling the American troops out of Berlin to avoid a clash.
Sending an armed convoy down the road into West Berlin to force it open.
Flying supplies into Berlin for months and holding the city without a shot.
Invading Eastern Europe to remove the communist governments.

questions.text: The Marshall Plan offered aid to all of Europe, yet Stalin forced the countries he controlled to refuse it. What was the effect?

answers.text: The plan failed everywhere in Europe.
Western Europe's economies stayed weak.
Communist parties gained ground in the West.
The aid went to Western Europe, where factories restarted and communist parties lost ground.

questions.text: Senator Robert Taft opposed the North Atlantic Treaty. Which concern did he hold?

answers.text: That the treaty cost too much money.
That it might drag the country into wars that Congress had not chosen.
That Britain and France could not be trusted.
That the Soviet Union would join NATO.

quizzes.description: Choose the best answer to each question. Some questions ask you to put together facts from different parts of the course.

questions.text: The United Nations gave each of five great powers a veto in the Security Council. What was the thinking behind this design?

answers.text: Small nations had asked for a veto, so the great powers took one too, to keep the balance of votes.
The veto let the General Assembly overrule the Security Council whenever a majority of nations wished.
No peace could last unless the great powers agreed, though the veto might stall the council at times.
The veto was meant to make wars easier to start by letting any member nation call for action at once.

questions.text: Which statement best describes George Kennan's policy of containment?

answers.text: Hold the line against Soviet expansion and wait, because a system built on fear and force would weaken within.
Roll back communism wherever it already ruled by sending armies into the countries that Stalin controlled.
Cut off all trade and talks with the Soviets and then wait for a war that could not be avoided for long.
Rebuild the economy of the Soviet Union with American aid so that its leaders would give up communism.

questions.text: During the Berlin blockade, Truman rejected both a withdrawal and an attempt to force a road through with troops. Why did the airlift fit his aims better?

answers.text: It let the United States take over East Berlin without Soviet leaders learning of it until too late.
It forced Stalin to withdraw his armies from Eastern Europe within a few weeks of the first flights.
It cost far less money than the Marshall Plan, and Congress had refused to pay for anything larger.
It kept West Berlin supplied and held the West's ground without a shot that might start a war.

questions.text: Truman sent American forces to Korea without asking Congress for a declaration of war. Why does this raise a question for a republic?

answers.text: The Constitution forbids the president from working with the United Nations in any matter of war.
The Constitution gives Congress the power to declare war, yet a major war was fought as a "police action."
Congress had already voted against sending troops, and Truman sent them anyway during the recess.
Truman had named a general to run the war, and the Constitution gives that power only to the Senate.

questions.text: Many historians say the republic passed a test when Truman fired General MacArthur. Which reason is correct?

answers.text: The Senate voted to restore MacArthur, and Truman agreed to let him widen the war against China.
MacArthur was proved to be a spy, and the Joint Chiefs gave the evidence to Congress in public hearings.
A popular general lost an argument with an elected president, and no one tried to override the result.
Truman won the next election by a large margin because the public had always opposed MacArthur.

questions.text: Which pair of facts best explains the rapid growth of the suburbs after the war?

answers.text: The GI Bill helped veterans buy homes, and builders such as Levitt used assembly-line methods to build houses fast.
Families disliked cities because of the bombing, and the Interstate Highways had already been finished by 1945.
Banks gave loans only to Black families, and the government forbade any building within city limits.
Factories moved to farmland after the war, and Congress ordered veterans to settle on the edge of cities.

questions.text: The NAACP's lawyers began by attacking the "equal" half of separate but equal in graduate schools, not Plessy itself. Why was that a sound plan?

answers.text: The Supreme Court had already said that it would overturn Plessy once graduate schools were integrated.
Showing that states could not provide truly equal schools chipped away at the system, one win at a time.
Graduate schools were the only schools in the South that were paid for with federal money at that time.
Southern governors had agreed to desegregate their graduate schools if the NAACP left grade schools alone.

questions.text: Eisenhower had not publicly endorsed Brown, yet he sent paratroopers to Little Rock. What was his reason?

answers.text: He had changed his mind about integration and wanted to show the South that he supported the decision.
The Supreme Court had ordered him to send troops and had given him a deadline of one week.
Congress had passed a law that required the president to protect every school from any mob.
A governor who defied a federal court was attacking the Constitution, so the matter was the rule of law.

questions.text: Which statement best explains how the Civil Rights Act of 1964 became law?

answers.text: The movement, the press, and a skillful president worked together, and Republican votes helped end the filibuster.
Southern senators voted for it at once, since they had promised Kennedy that they would not resist.
Johnson signed it by executive order after the Senate had refused to bring it to a vote for fifty days.
The Supreme Court wrote the law itself and sent it to Congress, which had only to approve it as written.

questions.text: Kennedy called the naval blockade of Cuba a "quarantine." What was his reason for choosing that word?

answers.text: A quarantine would be easier to explain to Congress, which had refused to approve the blockade.
The Soviet Union had asked him to avoid the word, and he agreed in return for the removal of the missiles.
Under international law, a blockade is an act of war, and he wanted to avoid that label.
The word was borrowed from health officials, who were the only ones allowed to stop Soviet ships.

questions.text: How was the Cuban Missile Crisis settled?

answers.text: Kennedy bombed the missile sites and invaded Cuba, and Khrushchev gave up when Castro was removed.
Kennedy answered the first letter and ignored the second, while privately promising to move the Turkey missiles.
Khrushchev agreed to leave the missiles in Cuba if Kennedy promised not to blockade the island again.
The United Nations ordered both sides to withdraw, and Cuba paid for the cost of the blockade.

questions.text: The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 is a good example of an unintended consequence. Why?

answers.text: Supporters expected a large increase in immigration from Europe, but the numbers from Europe fell to zero.
Supporters wanted to keep the quotas of the 1920s, but the Supreme Court struck down the new law.
Supporters expected immigration to end, but the law gave a priority to those with family ties abroad.
Supporters expected few immigrants from outside Europe, but immigration shifted greatly toward Asia and Latin America.

questions.text: Eisenhower's domino theory was a guess about the future that no one could prove. What was the theory?

answers.text: That if one country got an atomic bomb, every country near it would build one in the next few years.
That if one country in a region fell to communism, its neighbors would fall one after another.
That if South Vietnam won its war, all of Asia would become friendly to the United States for a long time.
That if the draft ended, American soldiers would leave Vietnam one by one until none were left there.

questions.text: What event led directly to the protests at Kent State University in May 1970?

answers.text: The assassination of Robert Kennedy in Los Angeles and the riots that followed in many cities.
The vote of Congress to end the draft and to begin an army made up of volunteers only.
Nixon's announcement that American troops had entered Cambodia, which set off campus protests.
The march on the Pentagon in 1967, where a hundred thousand protesters came to Washington.

questions.text: A public school that receives federal money spends heavily on boys' sports but cuts all girls' teams. Which law is most directly aimed at this problem?

answers.text: Title IX of 1972, which banned sex discrimination in education programs that receive federal money.
The Voting Rights Act of 1965, which banned literacy tests and sent in federal examiners.
The Wagner Act of 1935, which protected the right of workers to organize and to bargain as a group.
The Equal Rights Amendment, which Congress sent to the states in 1972 and which became law in 1980.

questions.text: Why did the opening to China give Nixon an advantage over the Soviet Union?

answers.text: China agreed to stop selling weapons to North Vietnam, which ended the war in Vietnam in 1972.
China joined NATO and sent troops to Europe, and so the Soviets had to move their army.
China gave up communism after Nixon's visit, and the Soviet Union lost its largest trading partner.
China and the Soviets distrusted each other, so Moscow now had to worry about its two largest rivals drawing closer.

questions.text: Which description fits the American economy after the oil embargo of 1973?

answers.text: Prices fell quickly because of lower demand, and unemployment fell as new factories were built.
Prices stayed the same, but wages rose so quickly that the government had to cap them by law.
Prices were rising fast while the economy was stuck and unemployment stayed high for years.
The economy grew faster than at any time in the century, but the cost of oil kept it from the top.

questions.text: A president refuses to hand over tapes that a court needs in a criminal case, and claims executive privilege. According to United States v. Nixon, what follows?

answers.text: Privilege exists but is not absolute, so his claim of secrecy must give way to the need for evidence.
A president has no privilege at all, so every presidential conversation must be made public.
A president's claim of privilege always wins, because the courts have no power to order the president.
The Court may not decide the matter, because only the House of Representatives can order the tapes.

questions.text: The Strategic Defense Initiative never worked in Reagan's time. Why did it still matter?

answers.text: It protected American cities from missile attack during the last years of the Cold War.
It showed Congress that the United States could win a war without ever using soldiers.
It led the Soviet Union to sign a treaty to end the arms race before the first test.
The Soviets took it seriously and feared they could not afford to match it or to answer it.

questions.text: Which action best fits the Reagan Doctrine?

answers.text: Signing a treaty with the Soviet Union that limited the number of missiles each side could build.
Sending American money and missiles to rebels who fought the Red Army in Afghanistan for a decade.
Sending American soldiers to occupy Nicaragua after Congress had declared war on the country.
Cutting taxes on businesses and high earners in the hope of faster growth in the economy.

questions.text: Gorbachev hoped glasnost would save the Soviet system. Why did it help to shake the system apart instead?

answers.text: Once people were allowed to talk, they said aloud what they long believed, and the party lost its power to frighten.
Glasnost allowed private business, and the new owners bought the factories from the state.
Glasnost ended the arms race, and the army then overthrew the government in the next year.
Glasnost gave the republics the right to vote, and all fifteen of them left on the same day.

questions.text: After the dot-com boom, an old lesson was learned again: speculation can run ahead of reality. Which events support this?

answers.text: The federal government took in less money than it spent, and unemployment rose to ten percent.
Banks refused to lend to internet firms, and the stock market had never risen above its level of 1990.
Investors poured money into any firm with ".com" in its name, and many internet firms failed in 2000 and 2001.
The Internet was used only by scientists, and companies could not find any customers for their goods.

questions.text: President Bush was popular after the Gulf War, yet he lost the election of 1992. Which factors help explain this?

answers.text: Congress had refused to authorize the war, and the voters blamed Bush for starting it.
The war had gone badly in its last weeks, and Saddam Hussein remained in power in Kuwait.
Bill Clinton had been in the Senate for twenty years, and the voters wanted a more experienced leader.
A downturn in the economy made voters worry about jobs, and Ross Perot took many votes from Bush.

questions.text: What did the Supreme Court decide in Bush v. Gore?

answers.text: By nine to zero, that Florida had to hold a new election in every county within a month.
By five to four, that the recount as done did not treat voters equally, and there was no time for a fair one.
By five to four, that Gore had won the popular vote and so should be named president.
By six to three, that the Electoral College was unconstitutional and the vote should be counted nationwide.

questions.text: Critics have compared the Authorization for Use of Military Force of 2001 to the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution. What do the two have in common?

answers.text: Both were declarations of war that named the country to be attacked and the date it would end.
Both passed by close votes after weeks of debate and were later repealed by the Supreme Court.
Both were written by the Senate alone, and neither one was signed by the president.
Both gave a president wide powers in a short time, and critics said Congress gave up too much of its role.

questions.text: Why did the war in Iraq turn into a long struggle after Saddam Hussein fell?

answers.text: The Iraqi army had kept fighting from the north, and the weapons of mass destruction were then found.
Congress ordered the troops home in 2003, and the United States left Iraq without any troops at all.
The government had no plan for ruling the country, the army was disbanded, and an insurgency spread.
Saddam escaped to Afghanistan, and the Taliban took over the government of Iraq before the surge.

questions.text: Which statement best describes the advice in Washington's Farewell Address, as historians explain it?

answers.text: Act abroad for the nation's own interests and peace, and guard unity at home against party spirit.
Never trade with foreign nations, and keep the army at home in every circumstance.
Join permanent alliances with Britain and France, and form political parties at home to guard liberty.
Make war on any country that threatens trade, and let the states decide how to treat foreign powers.

quizzes.title: Semester Final
quizzes.description: This final covers all of Quarters 3 and 4. It is optional. Choose the best answer to each question. Some questions ask you to put together facts from different parts of the course.

questions.text: Wilson tied the League of Nations to the Treaty of Versailles itself. Why did that choice hurt the League in the Senate?

answers.text: The treaty had to be approved by a vote of the American people before the Senate could take up the League at all.
The Senate could not approve one without the other, so objections to the treaty also threatened the League.
Britain and France refused to sign the treaty unless the Senate first agreed to every one of Lodge's changes.
Wilson's own party had left the League out of the treaty, so it had to be settled later in separate talks at Geneva.

questions.text: Supporters of the immigration laws of the 1920s made a serious argument in the language of a republic. Which argument did they make?

answers.text: Nearly all newcomers belonged to the Communist Party, so each one who arrived brought the Bolshevik revolution closer to America.
Earlier immigrants had been feared too and had still become Americans, so the quotas would only be needed for a short time.
Every republic must admit at least three percent more people each year from every country, or its citizens will lose their liberty.
A republic needs citizens who share loyalties, language, and habits, and too many strangers can strain schools and wages.

questions.text: By the 1920s the Model T cost under $300. Which combination of methods best explains how Ford cut costs so far?

answers.text: Interchangeable parts, a moving assembly line, and timed "one best way" methods for each job.
Hand-fitted parts made by skilled craftsmen, one building spot for each car, and long hours of unpaid overtime for every worker.
A move to cheaper foreign workers, a smaller plant at Highland Park, and a ban on every kind of labor union in his factories.
Government loans from the General Motors Acceptance Corporation, free steel from federal mines, and lower taxes on car sales.

questions.text: Treasury Secretary Andrew Mellon pushed for lower taxes on the highest incomes. What reasoning did he give?

answers.text: Lower taxes would persuade farmers to leave the countryside and take jobs on the new assembly lines in the cities.
Higher taxes on the poor would end the need for installment buying and for the credit plans offered by car makers.
The wealthy had paid too little during the war, and a lower rate would let Congress correct that mistake over time.
Lower taxes would encourage people to invest and build, which would help the whole economy grow.

questions.text: Radio, movies, and national sports heroes created a mass culture. The lesson says this may have helped the republic. How?

answers.text: Millions of people shared the same stories, songs, and heroes, which can build affection beyond their own towns.
National programs replaced local traditions, which ended the need for citizens to take part in local self-government.
Paid advertising on the air taught listeners to restrain their appetites and to save money before they bought anything.
The government ran American radio, as in Britain, and used broadcasts to teach every citizen the Constitution each week.

questions.text: The Ku Klux Klan grew rapidly in the 1920s but fell apart by the end of the decade. Which event helped bring it down?

answers.text: A federal law passed in 1924 that made membership in the Klan a crime in every state of the Union.
The Scopes Trial, in which Clarence Darrow proved that its members had never read the Bible they praised.
The repeal of Prohibition, which cut off the money that Klan members had been earning from bootlegging.
Scandals, including the 1925 murder conviction of an Indiana Klan leader named D. C. Stephenson.

questions.text: Hoover opposed direct federal handouts to the poor. Which belief stood behind that view?

answers.text: The Constitution forbade federal relief, and the Supreme Court had said so in a ruling made in 1930.
Such handouts would weaken the independence and character of citizens.
Private charities and local governments had grown large enough to meet every need without further help.
The Reconstruction Finance Corporation would soon give every unemployed worker a monthly check for life.

questions.text: During the Depression, many Mexican Americans in the Southwest faced a special pressure. What was it?

answers.text: Federal law required that Mexican workers be hired first for relief jobs on every new public works project.
Their farms were taken by the government and added to the Dust Bowl lands of the Great Plains.
Officials pushed families to leave the country, a policy called repatriation, even when many were citizens.
Their children were barred from every public school by an order that Hoover signed in 1932.

questions.text: Roosevelt said in the 1932 campaign, "It is common sense to take a method and try it. If it fails, admit it frankly and try another." What did this approach mean for the Hundred Days?

answers.text: The New Deal had no single theory, and some of its laws pulled in opposite directions.
Congress followed one plan written in advance, so every law of 1933 raised federal spending and prices.
Roosevelt dropped each program as soon as a critic objected, so almost none of the laws remained.
The Brain Trust wrote the laws without the president, and Congress passed them after months of debate.

questions.text: Under the Agricultural Adjustment Act, payments for cutting crops went mostly to landowners. What happened to many Southern tenants and sharecroppers as a result?

answers.text: Tenants received most of the payments and used them to buy the land that they had farmed for years.
Tenants were given the right to bargain as a union with their landlords under the new law.
Many owners used the money to buy machines and to evict their tenants.
The Civilian Conservation Corps hired every evicted sharecropper and paid each one the same wage.

questions.text: John L. Lewis wanted to organize everyone in a big industry, from skilled to unskilled workers. How did the Wagner Act help him?

answers.text: It ended the strike at Flint by ordering General Motors to sell its plants to the workers who held them.
It protected the right to organize and required employers to bargain, so his new group could grow.
It set a minimum wage of twenty-five cents an hour, which led workers to join unions in huge numbers.
It banned unions of skilled craftsmen, so that only unions covering a whole industry could survive.

questions.text: Schechter Poultry v. United States struck down a law passed during the Hundred Days. What had that law allowed businesses in each industry to do?

answers.text: Pay farmers to grow less so that the prices of crops would rise again.
Write codes of fair competition that set prices, wages, and hours.
Insure the savings of customers whenever a bank failed in their town.
Build dams on a river to control floods and make cheap electricity.

questions.text: The Nye Committee argued that bankers and arms makers had pushed the country into the Great War. Historians now think its case was weak. Why did it still matter?

answers.text: Many Americans believed it, and that strengthened isolationism in the 1930s.
Its report led Congress to join the League of Nations so that no future war could start.
It proved that the Neutrality Acts had been written by the owners of arms factories.
It convinced Roosevelt to ask Congress for a declaration of war on Italy and Japan.

questions.text: In August 1941, Roosevelt and Churchill issued the Atlantic Charter. What did it promise?

answers.text: That the United States would enter the war within a month and send an army to Britain.
That Germany would be divided into zones and that Poland would hold free elections.
No new territory for either nation, free choice of governments, and free seas.
That the Axis powers would be offered peace if they gave up Czechoslovakia and Austria.

questions.text: For most of three years, the Soviet army bore the weight of the war on land against Germany. Which pair of facts best supports this statement?

answers.text: The Soviets landed at Normandy in 1942, and the Americans took Berlin before the winter was over.
The Soviets lost the battle of Stalingrad, and the Americans sent them no trucks, food, or fuel.
The Soviets destroyed a German army at Stalingrad, and the West could not yet open a second front.
Stalin signed the Atlantic Charter first, and the Soviets held the Kasserine Pass against the Germans.

questions.text: American commanders used a plan called island hopping in the Pacific. What did this plan do?

answers.text: It took some islands for airfields and skipped others, leaving their defenders cut off.
It captured every Japanese-held island in order, starting at Iwo Jima and ending at Guadalcanal.
It used Navajo code talkers to pass messages from island to island so that no ship needed radio.
It sent bombers from Saipan to Tokyo while the Marines stayed at sea until the war was over.

questions.text: In 1941, A. Philip Randolph threatened to bring one hundred thousand Black marchers to Washington. What did Roosevelt do in response?

answers.text: He banned discrimination in defense industries and set up a committee to enforce the ban.
He ordered the armed forces to end segregation and to open every unit to Black soldiers and sailors.
He asked Congress to pass the Fair Labor Standards Act and to promise equal pay to Black workers.
He called out the army to stop the marchers and had Randolph arrested on the steps of the Capitol.

questions.text: The Potsdam Declaration of July 1945 told Japan to surrender at once but did not say what would happen to the emperor. Why did that silence matter?

answers.text: It meant that the Soviet Union alone would decide the emperor's fate at a meeting held later that summer.
It showed that Truman had already decided to invade Kyushu in the spring, before the declaration was written.
It proved that Japan had already surrendered in secret, and that only a formal signing was left to do.
The emperor's future was a key question for Japan's leaders, so the silence made surrender harder to accept.

questions.text: After 1945, the Red Army drove the Germans out of Eastern Europe and stayed. What was the result in countries such as Poland and Hungary?

answers.text: Free elections were held under American watch, and the new governments soon joined the North Atlantic alliance.
Each country took a seat on the Security Council with a veto of its own, backed by the Soviet Union.
Local communists backed by Soviet power took control, and the countries became satellite states.
The Marshall Plan rebuilt their factories, and their trade with the West grew faster than anywhere else.

questions.text: In April 1950, NSC-68 urged a large increase in American military spending. Which event soon seemed to prove its argument?

answers.text: The start of the Korean War within three months.
The Soviet blockade of Berlin, which began in June of the year 1948.
The launch of Sputnik by the Soviet Union in the autumn of 1957.
The first Soviet test of an atomic bomb in the late summer of 1949.

questions.text: Senator Joseph McCarthy lost his power after 1954. Which event did the most to turn the public against him?

answers.text: The conviction of Alger Hiss for lying under oath, which proved that McCarthy's charges had been false.
Televised hearings in which he attacked the Army and appeared to be a bully.
The execution of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, after which he apologized to the Senate for his charges.
The speech by Margaret Chase Smith, which led the Senate to vote him out of office the next day.

questions.text: The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 was defended partly as a matter of national defense. Which effect on cities does the lesson also describe?

answers.text: The highways were paid for by a tax on cars and trucks, which closed the city bus lines.
The highways made it too costly to live far from work, so families moved back to the cities.
The highways cut through many city neighborhoods, usually poor ones.
The highways were built only in the South, where the federal government had the most land.

questions.text: In 1955, the Court told local school boards to desegregate "with all deliberate speed." How did Southern officials use that phrase?

answers.text: They treated the wording as permission to delay; ten years later few Black children in the Deep South attended school with white children.
They used it to desegregate every school in the state within one year, and a decade later nearly all Black children were enrolled in them.
They used it to ask Congress for an amendment to the Constitution, and a decade later the amendment had been ratified in every state.
They used it to end the segregated bus seating of Montgomery, and a decade later buses in the Deep South were fully mixed.

questions.text: Martin Luther King Jr. held that nonviolence was a moral principle. The lesson also calls it a smart strategy. Why?

answers.text: Southern juries would not convict any person who had been attacked by a marcher who stayed peaceful and polite.
The Supreme Court had ruled that only nonviolent protests were allowed under the First Amendment in the South.
A small, quiet movement could be ignored by President Kennedy until the courts had finished their work in each case.
When peaceful marchers were beaten by police, the injustice of the system was plain to the whole country.

questions.text: The invasion at the Bay of Pigs failed in April 1961. What did Kennedy learn from it?

answers.text: He learned that Congress would declare war on any country that took American property.
He learned to be more careful about what the military and the CIA told him.
He learned that Cubans would rise up if American planes supported another landing.
He learned that the Soviet Union would never place weapons so close to the American coast.

questions.text: Johnson signed Medicare in Independence, Missouri, with Harry Truman beside him. Why was that a fitting place and guest?

answers.text: Truman had signed the Social Security Act in the same town in the year 1935.
Truman had proposed national health insurance twenty years before.
Independence had been the first city in the country to enroll its elderly citizens.
Truman had been the vice president when the first version of Medicare was written.

questions.text: South Vietnam's leader, Ngo Dinh Diem, was overthrown in November 1963. What does the lesson say about the coup?

answers.text: The Viet Cong overthrew him in a night attack, and the Marines landed at Da Nang the next week.
The Senate voted to remove him after the Gulf of Tonkin attack proved that he had lied to Congress.
Generals overthrew and killed him after the United States signaled it would not stop them.
North Vietnamese tanks drove him from Saigon, and the fighting in the country ended not long after.

questions.text: Several movements of the 1960s borrowed methods from the civil rights movement. Which pair is correct?

answers.text: Berkeley students used sit-ins, and farmworkers used a grape boycott and nonviolent protest.
Berkeley students used the Montgomery bus boycott, and farmworkers used the sit-down strike at Flint.
Antiwar protesters used the Freedom Rides, and farmworkers used a filibuster to pass a labor law.
American Indian activists used a march from Selma, and Berkeley students used a grape boycott.

questions.text: The War Powers Resolution of 1973 tried to answer a question that the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution had left open. What was that question?

answers.text: Whether the president may fire a special prosecutor who is looking into a crime.
Whether South Vietnam or North Vietnam should rule the whole divided country.
Whether the draft should go on once an all-volunteer army was ready to take its place.
Who decides when America goes to war, and for how long it may fight.

questions.text: A month after taking office, Gerald Ford gave Richard Nixon a full pardon. How did many Americans react?

answers.text: They cheered, because the House had already voted to remove Nixon from office a week before.
They demanded that Ford resign, and he left office within the year after a vote in the Senate.
They ignored it, because the Supreme Court had already ruled that the pardon was unconstitutional.
They were furious and suspected a secret deal, though no evidence of one was ever found.

questions.text: In the Iran-Contra affair, staff members used profits from secret arms sales to Iran to pay for the Contras. Why was that against the law?

answers.text: Congress had banned all trade with Iran under the War Powers Resolution of 1973.
The Constitution forbids a president from naming any adviser on national security.
Congress had banned military aid to the Contras.
The Supreme Court had ruled in United States v. Nixon that arms sales must be made public.

questions.text: SALT I in 1972 limited the number of missiles each side could build. How was the 1987 Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty different?

answers.text: It ended the Strategic Defense Initiative, which both sides agreed was against the treaty.
It allowed no inspections, since each side promised to trust the other without checking.
It set a ratio of five to three for the largest warships that each nation could keep.
It destroyed a whole class of nuclear weapons instead of only limiting their growth.

questions.text: In 1996, Clinton signed a law that reformed welfare. What did it do?

answers.text: It created health care for the elderly and for the poor, paid for in part by the states.
It ended the quota system and gave priority to family ties and to skills.
It set time limits on benefits and required recipients to work.
It banned the knowing hiring of people without legal status and offered amnesty.

questions.text: The Oklahoma City bombing of 1995 killed 168 people. What does the lesson say about the person who carried it out?

answers.text: He was a member of al-Qaeda, which showed that the group could strike inside the country.
He was an American-born man, which showed that terrorists could be homegrown.
He had arrived from abroad, which led Congress to tighten the quotas on immigrants again.
He was an agent of the FBI, which showed that the agencies had failed to share their reports.

questions.text: After September 11, Congress passed the USA PATRIOT Act. What did critics say about it?

answers.text: It took away the power of the Senate to approve treaties, which the Constitution gives to the Senate alone.
It gave the government powers that threatened liberty and protection against unreasonable searches.
It ended the use of the Electoral College, which the Constitution requires for presidential elections.
It allowed the president to declare war on any nation, which the Constitution gives to the courts to decide.

questions.text: In 1796, George Washington warned against "permanent alliances" with foreign nations. Which action in the Cold War did the lessons describe as a step that he had warned against?

answers.text: Joining the League of Nations in 1920, as its first member and its leading voice.
Passing the Neutrality Acts of the 1930s, which kept ships out of war zones.
Signing the Limited Test Ban Treaty in 1963, which banned nuclear tests in the air.
Joining NATO in 1949, a binding military alliance made in peacetime.

quizzes.title: EOC Practice Exam
quizzes.description:
About this practice exam. This practice exam is optional and does not count toward your grade. It covers only part of what the full End-of-Course test covers: the topics from Quarters 3 and 4, from the 1920s through the early twenty-first century. It leaves out the earlier topics, so a good score here does not predict how you would do on every topic. Use it to practice reading sources and answering questions in the style of the End-of-Course test.

Read each question and choose the best answer.

questions.text:
Read the information and answer the question.

1919: The Senate votes down the Treaty of Versailles with changes added by Senator Lodge.

1919: The Senate votes down the treaty with no changes.

March 1920: A third vote falls short of the needed two-thirds.

July 1921: Congress ends the state of war with Germany.

1921 to 1922: The United States hosts the Washington Naval Conference.

Which conclusion about American foreign policy in the early 1920s does this timeline best support?

answers.text: The nation turned away from every international agreement and refused to meet with other powers.
The Senate approved the treaty in 1920 and then joined the League when the war was ended.
The nation left the peace talks and signed a separate treaty with each member of the League.
The nation stayed out of the League but still made major agreements with other powers.

questions.text:
Read the information and answer the question.

Washington Naval Conference treaty (1922): For every five tons of battleships that Britain or the United States kept, Japan could keep three.

What was the main purpose of this agreement?

answers.text: To give Japan the largest navy in the world in exchange for its help in the Great War.
To make the League of Nations pay for the ships that each country agreed to scrap.
To force Britain to give up its navy so that the United States could rule the oceans.
To limit the largest warships so the great naval powers would not race to build more.

questions.text:
Read the information and answer the question.

Immigration to the United States

Before the Emergency Quota Act of 1921: more than 800,000 people a year

After the Act: about 357,000 people a year

Which development best explains the change shown?

answers.text: A new war in Europe made it too dangerous for most people to cross the Atlantic.
Growing nativism after the war led Congress to set fixed limits for each country.
The Supreme Court ruled that every immigrant after 1910 had entered the country illegally.
The Great Migration of Black families led to the closing of the southern ports of entry.

questions.text:
Read the information and answer the question.

January 1920: Federal agents arrest thousands of people in more than thirty cities, many without warrants.

A Labor Department official, Louis F. Post, reviews the deportation cases and cancels many orders.

Judges and a group of prominent lawyers criticize the raids.

Which statement best describes the difficulty that these events show for a republic?

answers.text: A government must keep order, but it must also rule by laws that treat everyone the same way.
A government must choose between the needs of farmers and the needs of workers in the cities.
A government must avoid every strike, because strikes always lead to the end of a republic.
A government must keep the Senate from approving any treaty with a foreign nation.

questions.text:
Read the information and answer the question.

1919: General Motors creates the General Motors Acceptance Corporation to lend money to car buyers.

By the end of the 1920s: Most new cars are sold on installment plans.

Throughout the 1920s: Household debt rises.

Which risk did this trend create for the American economy?

answers.text: Banks would be forced to lend money only to the wealthy, since they could not afford to take any risks.
Car prices would rise above $850, since buyers could no longer pay cash for any car.
Family spending came to depend on incomes that could vanish if jobs and wages fell.
Factories would stop making consumer goods, since workers would refuse to buy things on credit.

questions.text:
Read the information and answer the question.

"I, too, sing America."

Langston Hughes, from the poem "I, Too," published during the Harlem Renaissance

What claim does the poet make with this line?

answers.text: Black Americans were part of the national story and not outsiders to it.
Black Americans should leave the cities of the North and return to the farms of the South.
Black Americans should form a separate nation and sail to Africa on Black-owned ships.
Black Americans had no reason to hope for a future in the United States of America.

questions.text:
Read the information and answer the question.

Between 1925 and September 1929, the average price of leading stocks more than tripled.

Many buyers paid only ten to twenty percent of a stock's price and borrowed the rest from a broker.

Why was buying stocks "on margin" so risky when prices began to fall?

answers.text: The government raised the price of every stock that was bought with borrowed money.
Brokers demanded repayment right away, and buyers who could not pay lost everything.
The brokers paid the buyers a bonus, which made the buyers sell their shares at once.
The buyers were required to hold their shares for ten years before they could sell them.

questions.text:
Read the information and answer the question.

June 1930: Congress passes the Smoot-Hawley Tariff, which raises rates on thousands of goods.

More than a thousand economists sign a petition asking Hoover to veto it.

Other countries answer with tariffs of their own.

Which result of the tariff is best supported by this information?

answers.text: American factories hired millions of new workers to supply the rising demand from other nations.
American prices fell sharply, because foreign goods were no longer taxed when they arrived.
American farmers and factories lost foreign customers they could not afford to lose.
American banks became safer, because the government insured every deposit at the same time.

questions.text:
Read the information and answer the question.

After the Great War: European nations owed large war debts to the United States.

Many European nations borrowed American money to rebuild.

When American lending dried up, the shock spread across the ocean.

What does this information suggest about the American economy in the 1920s?

answers.text: It was cut off from Europe, so a crisis abroad could not reach American banks.
It was tied closely to Europe, so a crisis in one place could spread to the other.
It was controlled by Europe, so the American Congress could not change its own tariffs.
It was growing so quickly that no country in Europe could afford to trade with America.

questions.text:
Read the information and answer the question.

March 4, 1933: Roosevelt takes office.

March 6: A bank holiday closes every bank in the country.

March 9: Congress passes the Emergency Banking Act in a single afternoon.

March 12: Roosevelt explains the plan by radio.

When the banks reopened, people put money back in.

Which conclusion about the banking crisis is best supported by this timeline?

answers.text: A long debate in Congress over each bank gave citizens time to learn which banks were sound.
The banks stayed closed for the rest of the year, and the government paid every depositor in cash.
The president waited for the Supreme Court to rule on his plan before he closed any banks.
Quick action and a plain explanation to the public restored confidence and ended the run.

questions.text:
Read the information and answer the question.

Unemployment during the New Deal years (approximate)

1933: about 25 percent

1937: about 14 percent

1938: nearly 19 percent

Which statement is best supported by these figures?

answers.text: The New Deal ended the Depression by 1937, and no later problem of any kind arose.
The New Deal caused unemployment to rise every year from the time it began in 1933.
Unemployment fell steadily every year, so the recession of 1937 and 1938 never took place.
Recovery was real but uneven, and the New Deal alone did not end the Depression.

questions.text:
Read the information and answer the question.

1934 to 1936: A Senate committee holds hearings and argues that bankers and arms makers had pushed America into the Great War.

1935 to 1937: Congress passes the Neutrality Acts.

The acts banned the sale of weapons to nations at war and kept American ships and citizens out of war zones.

Which belief most likely shaped the Neutrality Acts?

answers.text: The League of Nations would protect the United States, so the country needed no policy of its own.
Avoiding the choices that led to war in 1917 would keep the country at peace.
Selling weapons to the Allied Powers would make Britain and France pay back their war debts.
The president should be free to send aid to any nation that asked for it, whatever the cost.

questions.text:
Read the information and answer the question.

Summer 1941: Japan moves troops into southern Indochina.

Roosevelt freezes Japanese money in American banks and cuts off oil.

Japan imported most of its oil from the United States.

December 7, 1941: Japanese planes attack Pearl Harbor.

Which statement best explains why Japan decided to attack the American fleet?

answers.text: Japan's leaders chose to take the oil of Southeast Asia by force and first destroy the American fleet.
Japan's leaders had signed a pact with the Soviet Union and no longer feared any attack from the Americans.
Japan's leaders wanted to win back the Philippines before the American army could reach the Pacific.
Japan's leaders had been promised oil by Germany and wanted to protect the shipping lanes to Europe.

questions.text:
Read the information and answer the question.

Before Midway, American codebreakers learned that Japan planned an attack on a target called "AF."

To prove that AF was Midway, the island sent out a false message that its water supply was low.

Soon after, the Japanese reported that "AF" was short of water.

Why did the Americans have Midway send the false message?

answers.text: To draw the Japanese carriers away from Hawaii and toward the island of Guadalcanal.
To warn the Japanese that the American carriers were low on fuel and could not fight.
To signal to the Navajo code talkers that the Marines were ready to land on the island.
To confirm that the target the Japanese called "AF" was Midway.

questions.text:
Read the information and answer the question.

"The very brink of constitutional power" and "the ugly abyss of racism."

Justice Frank Murphy, dissenting in Korematsu v. United States (1944)

Which concern is Justice Murphy expressing?

answers.text: The order was too weak to protect the West Coast from an invasion by the Japanese navy.
The order gave the Supreme Court too much power to decide cases in time of war.
The order treated a whole group of citizens as suspect because of ancestry, not proof.
The order forced the army to remove people from places that were not important for defense.

questions.text:
Read the information and answer the question.

"I believe that it must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures."

President Harry Truman, address to Congress, March 12, 1947

Which situation led directly to this promise?

answers.text: Britain told Washington that it could no longer aid Greece, and Turkey was under Soviet pressure.
Stalin cut off every road, rail line, and canal into West Berlin and left the city without supplies.
North Korean tanks crossed the 38th parallel and took Seoul within a few days of the attack.
Communists led by Mao Zedong won the civil war and took control of the mainland of China.

questions.text:
Read the information and answer the question.

1950: North Korean forces cross the 38th parallel.

September 1950: The Inchon landing breaks the North Korean army.

November 1950: Hundreds of thousands of Chinese soldiers attack, and UN forces retreat.

Early 1951: The front settles near the 38th parallel.

Why did Truman refuse General MacArthur's request to widen the war against China?

answers.text: He believed that Congress had already voted to give the war to the control of the United Nations.
He believed that China had signed a treaty ending the fighting along the Yalu River.
He had decided to use atomic weapons against North Korea and wanted no other army in the way.
He feared that a wider war might bring in the Soviet Union and become a third world war.

questions.text:
Read the information and answer the question.

Homeownership in the United States: under 45 percent in 1940; over 60 percent in 1960.

At Levittown, the builders at first refused to sell homes to Black buyers.

Federal lending practices often favored white neighborhoods and marked Black neighborhoods as risky.

Which conclusion about postwar prosperity is best supported by this information?

answers.text: The gains were shared equally, because federal lending favored every neighborhood the same way.
